name: Dana Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we don't sell anything. Everything stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Well, it's a working night, really. I'm on the slicing and bagging line at the big bakery on Station Road, ten at night to six in the morning, and we turn out something like forty thousand loaves a shift. I watch the slicer blades, feed bags onto the bagger, clear the jams when a loaf comes through squashed, and do the metal detector checks every hour with the little test sticks. I'm two years in and still the one they send to the easy end, which is fair, because I panic when the bagger jams twice in a row.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to the bakery?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fifteen years at the supermarket, deputy on the bakery counter funnily enough, and the pay just never moved. The factory paid a good bit more for nights, and with Femi's electrical work being up and down, we needed the steady money. What I like is the smell, honestly, I come home smelling of warm bread. What I don't like is sleeping in the day while Grace is home on the weekend wanting to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a useful gadget and that's it. I'd probably share some funny meme about robots in the family group chat. Life goes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can keep getting better on the line without looking over my shoulder. I've got plans to move to the mixing room, which pays a bit more. So no complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Ask Hamid, the shift leader, to put me on the mixer training when it comes up, and keep putting our hundred a month in savings. We've got about three months of bills covered, and I want to get that to four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's what I expect anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, now and then. I ask it to plan the week's dinners when I'm too tired to think, and once I got it to explain my payslip after a shift premium went missing. It was right, too, and I got the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the bakery you'd want to change in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moving off nights, eventually, so I can see Grace's netball on a Saturday. That's the main thing.

S0.say: It's a useful gadget and that's it. She'd share a funny robot meme in the family group chat and carry on.
S0.think: She can keep getting better on the line without looking over her shoulder, and she has plans to move to the better-paid mixing room. She has no complaints.
S0.do: Asks the shift leader for mixer training when it comes up and keeps saving a hundred a month. Aims to grow the family's three months of savings to four.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's what she expects anyway.
S0.quote: I got it to explain my payslip after a shift premium went missing. It was right, too, and I got the money.
S0.fieldNote: Dana uses AI for practical household tasks and once won back missing pay with it, so she's neither scared of it nor excited. Her goals are concrete: the mixing room and getting off nights. The plateau feels like her default expectation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we need to keep up, but also the company should train us rather than replace us. I'd say both, because both are true. I'm not one for picking sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the bagging end is already half automatic, and the bit I do is the bit they haven't got round to. I'd want to be in the mixing room before they do. The mixers need someone who knows dough, and I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the mixer training within the first six months and do a food safety course at the college if it helps. We'd put another fifty a month aside. And I'd start using the AI more, once I saw the shift leaders using it for scheduling, because then it'd be part of the job anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, just alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think happens to the bagging line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bagger gets a robot to stack the trays and a camera to check the seals, I'd bet. Then they need maybe two people where there's five. I'd rather not be the third one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you pick up technology once others have. Who would you be watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamid, mainly, the shift leader. If he starts using it and it works, I'll follow. He's careful, so if he trusts it, it's proven.

S1.say: It's a big change and workers need to keep up, but the company should train people rather than replace them. She'd say both, because both are true and she doesn't pick sides.
S1.think: Her part of the bagging line is the bit they haven't automated yet, so she wants to get into the mixing room before they do. The mixers need someone who knows dough, and she does.
S1.do: Pushes for mixer training within six months and takes a food safety course if it helps. Saves another fifty a month and starts using AI more once the shift leaders use it for scheduling.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy and alert, but not scared.
S1.quote: Then they need maybe two people where there's five. I'd rather not be the third one.
S1.fieldNote: Dana's centrist instinct shows in refusing to pick a side between keeping up and protecting workers. She has a clear move ready, toward the mixing room and her dough knowledge. She waits for a careful colleague to prove a tool before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is serious and people need help, not lectures. The government would have to do something, and fast. But I wouldn't be on a placard, I'd be at home working out bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be gone early. A bakery that's mostly machines already will go all the way the minute a robot can clear a jam. And the mixing room plan goes out the window too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop anything that isn't the mortgage, food and the kids' school things. I'd ask the bank early about lowering the payments. And I'd look for work near people, maybe back at a care home or the school kitchens, while there's still some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Proper stomach-dropping alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with Femi and work out exactly how long we'd last. Probably three months, maybe a bit more if his jobs keep coming. Then I'd talk to the bank before the first payment was late, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Femi's work is up and down already. How would the two of you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Femi reckons people will still want a person to rewire their old house for a while. Maybe. If he's working and I'm not, we'd live small. If we're both out, I don't know.

S2.say: This is serious and people need help, not lectures, so the government would have to act fast. She'd be at home working out bills rather than carrying a placard.
S2.think: A bakery that's already mostly machines would go all the way once a robot can clear a jam, so she'd be gone early. Her plan for the mixing room would vanish too.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the mortgage, food and school costs and asks the bank early about lower payments. Looks for work near people, such as a care home or school kitchen, while it lasts.
S2.quote: A bakery that's mostly machines already will go all the way the minute a robot can clear a jam.
S2.fieldNote: Her practical side takes over immediately: counting months of savings and calling the bank before missing a payment. She hopes her electrician husband's work lasts longer but isn't sure. Her public stance stays measured even when she's frightened privately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so get ready. Learn something, save something. That's what I'd tell my sister and anyone at work who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get into the mixing room and earn a bit more before it all changes. Then I'd want to be heading somewhere else by year four. I just don't know where yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the mixer training straight away and save the extra pay, maybe a hundred and fifty more a month. In year two or three I'd look at a care course or something with people. I'd use the AI to research which jobs are holding up, and check what my cousin in the hospital says too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three more years than the last one. What does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to save, mainly, and time for Tobi to finish school before it hits. With two years he'd be leaving school into nothing. With five, at least he can pick a direction knowing what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tobi about his own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't pick something just because it pays now. Pick something where people need a person. He wants to do computer games, and I don't know how to tell him that might not be there.

S3.say: There are a few years, so get ready: learn something and save something. She'd tell her sister and anyone at work who asked.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get into the mixing room and earn more before everything changes. By year four she'd want to be heading somewhere else, though she doesn't yet know where.
S3.do: Starts mixer training straight away and saves about a hundred and fifty more a month. Looks at a care course in year two or three and uses AI, plus her cousin's advice, to see which jobs are holding up.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, and being busy helps.
S3.quote: He wants to do computer games, and I don't know how to tell him that might not be there.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns the mixing room into a stepping stone rather than a destination. Her son's career choice is the hardest part for her. She cross-checks what AI tells her with family who work in the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, ten years is plenty, let's plan it properly. No panicking, no pretending it won't happen. Sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is actually a decent amount of time. I'd get the mixing room, save, and then retrain in my late forties. I'd be 53 when it arrives, and I'd want to be somewhere it reaches last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same start, mixer training and saving. Then a proper care qualification in year four or five, part-time, while I'm still at the bakery. And I'd pay off a chunk of the mortgage so we're not stuck if one of us loses work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is there anything you'd do differently from the five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the care course slower, at my own pace, and not rush. I'd also let Tobi go for his games idea and change later if he needs to. Ten years is long enough for him to try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself working in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a care home, or helping in a school. Somewhere a person still matters. Honestly, I'd miss the smell of bread.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so plan it properly, without panicking or pretending it won't happen. She'd keep it to sensible steps and say so to anyone who asked.
S4.think: Ten years is a decent amount of time to get the mixing room, save and retrain in her late forties. She'd want to be in work that AGI reaches last by the time she's 53.
S4.do: Starts with mixer training and saving, then takes a part-time care qualification in year four or five while still at the bakery. Pays off a chunk of the mortgage and lets her son try his games plan.
S4.quote: I'd want to be somewhere it reaches last.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Dana sequences her moves calmly and even relaxes about her son's games ambitions. Her plan to pay down the mortgage shows she thinks in household terms. Her last comment about missing the smell of bread showed an attachment to the work she rarely voices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: 2028, because there's no time to do anything sensible. What would help is the bank giving families a break on the mortgage while they sort themselves out, and short courses for care or school work you can do around shifts. And some honesty from the company about what's coming, so I'm not hearing it from the rumour mill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Night workers, maybe. Nobody thinks about us. If they're going to change everything, I'd like it to be someone thinking about the people who are asleep when the meetings happen.

headlineQuote: I'd like it to be someone thinking about the people who are asleep when the meetings happen.
portrait: Dana Okafor, 43, works nights on the slicing and bagging line at a large bakery after fifteen years on a supermarket bakery counter. She uses AI now and then for meal plans and once to recover a missing pay premium, and waits for her careful shift leader to prove new tools. She refuses to pick sides publicly and thinks in household budgets, aiming for the mixing room and later care work. Fast AGI alarms her and sends her straight to the bank, while five or ten years let her plan step by step and loosen up about her son's dream.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to do anything sensible.
whatWouldHelp: Mortgage breaks for families while they adjust, short care or school courses that fit around shifts, and honesty from the company about what's coming.
